POV: you’re 34 years old and your brief career as a self-made solo AI entrepreneur / CEO / B2B SaaS founder is finally over.

You’re back in corporate, working a mid-level job at a fintech whose app occasionally duplicates transactions and shows negative balances.

The market changed. Two years ago recruiters begged you to “just have a conversation.” Now you’ve exhausted your entire network to land $180k TC.

And… it’s actually kind of nice.

There are snacks in the office. Free coffee. The sparkling water fridge is always full. You order a better Uber without guilt because you have a salary again.

You move Jira tickets around a little. Claude got smarter and can vibe-code half your tasks before your manager realizes it.

Suddenly you have free time. More importantly, you have money.

Your wife stops asking when the startup is going to make revenue. You send her to Barry’s with her friends while you stay late at the office “working.”

Before flying home from your first vacation in two years, she gets brunch with the girls in Palo Alto.

Maybe the real exit was getting a W-2.

Turns out meditation actually increases your "frame per second" of observing reality, allowing you to feel less time and more presence, which means you also take in & process more data. This is also why life feels "more" and "more real" for meditators (and the opposite, the more you're dissociated, I think).

I remember this weird Russian entrepreneur+biohacker guy who wore hearing aids (to enhance his hearing - he actually had no hearing problems) so he'd be able to negotiate better - bc he'd catch people's smallest tonality changes and whatnot and knew where to push/pull, etc. Imagine that kind of a leveling up, but for your full 5 senses - and more, we shall not talk about here.

Makes you way more here, way more real, way more able, and so on. Truly the limitless pill, but better. I wonder where it starts to asymptote if at all.

candidates.text:
Potentially unique situation here that maybe only a few people will fully understand but it's been on my mind recently and want to think out loud a bit

Anyways general gist is I feel like there's this secret third category of "unemployed guy" that the world doesn't really know how to relate with or give advice to. Where this guy is somewhat of a walking paradox. Doesn't have a job but does well for himself. Has nothing to do but always doing something

I am one of those guys. And honestly I'm at a point in my life where I don't want to be one of those guys anymore. To provide some context over the last five years or so I've essentially supported myself through just sharing my interests online. In other words I post about what I'm into. People connect with me on it. Then I find a way to monetize it

This might elicit some eye rolls but fortunately and unfortunately this has almost always led to immediate success. Had an arc where I was obsessed with coaching. Most recently another arc helping people settle into NYC. The home services idea I recently tweeted about. Trading crypto, launching a perfume, multitude of experiences that all worked

On paper that's not supposed to happen though. I'm not supposed to bounce around from shiny object to shiny object and make enough every time to be relatively free financially. But the universe keeps telling me "bro you lowkey have the magic touch" so I just continue to lean into and leverage it

A lot more I can say but dominant feeling is when I envision my life 5, 10, etc years from now, I don't find as much value in this type of lifestyle anymore. Taught me so much about myself throughout my 20's but definitely not something that invigorates me when I think about the version of me once I have kids. My desire to actually commit to something is stronger than ever right now

And I know that the best outcomes take time. Past decade was indirectly spent collecting self confidence, self belief, niche skills, etc but those are mostly intangible assets. Now I want to be able to look back in the long term and say that I actually believed in a mission, a vision, something much greater than myself. Growing that out with a team year over year. Joining an existing one and feeling like I'm a core piece of something meaningful. Instead of being 40 and still looking for the next cook

The compounding has to start this year. Recognize my high agency but tame and focus it a lot more. Yes "I can just do things" but doesn't mean I alway should. Acknowledge the abundance of options but strategically kill that optionality. Embrace the natural shift in priorities as a perpetually evolving human. I will figure it out. In the meantime, can only continue being grateful and trusting God's plan

candidates.text:
WHAT EUPHORIA LOOKS LIKE

I remember the Dotcom cycle vividly. 

The Netscape IPO was the wakeup call. 

I remember Gateway and Dell becoming household brands. 

Books A Million went up a gazillion percent on Thanksgiving week. 

3Com spin-off (top signal). 

The Goldman IPO (top signal). 

I remember partners at McKinsey daytrading stocks. 

I remember the book the 
‘New New Thing’ by Jim Barksdale. 

I remember everyone wanted to be a VC. 

I remember going to a lavish Global Crossing event and wondering why they were letting a college kid like me in. 

(Answer: ‘It’s all about eyeballs’). 

I remember Frank Quattrone at Credit Suisse was a legend. 

So was Mary Meeker and Henry Blodget. 

I remember the investment banker at JP Morgan not knowing what Geocities did. 

I remember Vertical Net saying their insane valuation meant that the market was telling them to do M&A and thinking how strange that sounded. 

I remember Doubleclick and the birth of Silicon Alley in NYC and Flatiron Partners. 

I remember Wall Street  investment bankers quitting to join startups. 

I remember Krispy Kreme going nuts in its IPO.  

I remember company issued press releases 
announcing a website causing stocks to surge. 

Where are we now?

Markets have memory. 

There is far more discipline in public markets today. 

There is also far more earnings growth, margin, and productivity growth. 

This is not a bubble. 

Too many of the leading companies have reasonable valuations matched with strong earnings growth.

We do not have a euphoria or ‘permanently higher plateau’. 

We have skepticism and a wall of worry. 

Check out the below snapsot in the newly launched ‘Feed’ Section of the Lumida Invest app (which triggered this post). 

It’s an infinite scroll that focuses solely on curated market insights.
